OCEANIA.title: Inflation jumps to 4.3%, adding to pressure for RBA rate rise next week
OCEANIA.simplified_title: Inflation jumps to 4.3%, making another interest rate rise likely
OCEANIA.quick_summary: Australia's annual inflation rose to 4.3% in September, driven by petrol and holiday costs, pushing markets to expect a fifth Reserve Bank rate rise this year on November 3.
OCEANIA.simplified_body:
Australia's annual inflation rate rose to 4.3% in September, up from 4.0% in August. The headline consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% for the month, mostly because petrol jumped 9.4% as world oil prices climbed. Domestic holiday travel and accommodation also rose 8.0%, thanks to school holidays and big sporting events. The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA's) favourite gauge, the trimmed mean, rose 1.0% for the quarter, which matched economists' expectations.

This matters for anyone with a mortgage or loan. Markets now see about an 80% chance the RBA lifts rates on Tuesday, which would be the fifth rise this year. That would take the cash rate from 4.60% to 4.85%, its highest in 18 years. Treasurer Jim Chalmers is also under pressure, with critics blaming government spending, while he points to global events and an investment boom in data centres.

Some background: inflation happens when demand outstrips what the economy can supply. Rate rises cool demand by making borrowing pricier. Back in 2022, the RBA and government hoped for a "soft landing", taming inflation without big job losses. ABC analysis argues that plan has now failed, partly due to a war hitting energy supplies and the AI investment boom. Not everything is overheating, though: housing inflation eased to 5.2% and unemployment is rising.

Next up is the RBA's November 3 decision and its updated forecasts. A pause would let earlier hikes work but wouldn't necessarily end the rate-rise cycle. Economists will also watch October's figures for the first effects of the card surcharge ban, which the RBA estimated could lift CPI by around 0.1% if businesses fold costs into prices.
OCEANIA.why_it_matters: Another rate rise would mean higher repayments for Australian borrowers already stretched by years of high prices, and the ABC warns tight conditions could last into 2027.
OCEANIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
This inflation episode began in 2022. The RBA and the government pursued what they called "the narrow path to a soft landing": raising rates less sharply than other countries to protect jobs. Historically, inflation has rarely been beaten without a recession, such as the one Paul Keating said Australia "had to have" in 1990. The cash rate now sits at 4.60% after four rises this year.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **The RBA:** Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser says the outlook has deteriorated substantially since August, citing energy prices and supply constraints, though he acknowledged weaker consumption and rising unemployment. Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter says demand is too strong relative to supply.
- **The Conversation:** Stresses nuance. Headline inflation was fuel-driven, underlying inflation matched forecasts, and a hold could give past hikes time to work.
- **ABC analysis:** More pessimistic, arguing the soft landing is likely out of reach and that demand will need suppressing well into 2027.
- **Government vs opposition:** Chalmers says global events and private investment are real causes and promises more savings. The opposition says the government could have been braver, pointing to EV and home battery discounts that benefited high-income earners.

## What to Watch
- The November 3 RBA decision and its updated forecasts.
- October inflation data, the first full month after the card surcharge ban.
- Unemployment trends and whether the government delivers promised savings.

options: It only measures petrol prices

OCEANIA.background_beginner: Inflation is how fast prices rise over time. In Australia, the Reserve Bank (RBA) tries to keep it between 2% and 3% a year. Its main tool is the cash rate: raising it makes loans more expensive, so people and businesses spend less, which eases pressure on prices. Since 2022, prices have been rising too fast, driven by global events, energy costs and strong demand. The RBA has raised rates several times, and the federal government, led on economics by Treasurer Jim Chalmers, faces criticism over its spending. The topic keeps coming up because every new inflation figure hints at whether mortgage repayments will climb again.
OCEANIA.description: Australia's annual inflation rose to 4.3% in September, driven by petrol and holiday costs, pushing markets to expect a fifth Reserve Bank rate rise this year on November 3.

OCEANIA.title: Australia records highest rates of anorexia and bulimia globally
OCEANIA.simplified_title: Australia has the world's highest rates of anorexia and bulimia
OCEANIA.quick_summary: A major global study published in JAMA Psychiatry found Australia has the highest rate of anorexia and bulimia in the world, while global cases have risen 71 per cent since 1990.
OCEANIA.simplified_body:
A new study published in the journal JAMA Psychiatry found Australia has the highest rate of anorexia and bulimia nervosa in the world, with an estimated 1,026.5 people per 100,000 living with one of the two eating disorders. Globally, cases have jumped 71 per cent since 1990, to about 18.1 million people as of 2023.

The disorders hit some groups harder. Females made up nearly 70 per cent of global cases, and about 41 per cent were young people aged 10 to 24. Lead researcher Damian Santomauro from the University of Queensland called Australia's ranking "surprising and concerning". He thinks social media and body image pressures may be one reason cases are rising. People from migrant backgrounds may also find it harder to get help.

The findings come from the Global Burden of Disease study, the world's largest health project. It measures how common illnesses are using surveys rather than treatment records, so it catches people who never get treated. Dr Santomauro said Australia's high number may be partly due to its surveys using a different method from other countries, though he doesn't think that explains it all. Butterfly Helpline psychologist Sarah Cox suggested Australia might simply be "seeing the problem more clearly". The study also only counted two disorders, so the true burden is bigger.

Researchers forecast cases will keep growing through to 2050. Experts are calling for more funding for early treatment and prevention, pointing to barriers such as cost, living in regional areas and stigma.
OCEANIA.why_it_matters: Australia tops the world for these two serious mental illnesses, and with cases forecast to keep rising, the pressure is on governments to fund earlier, more accessible treatment, especially for young people and those in regional areas.
OCEANIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
The Global Burden of Disease study began collecting data in 1990, and was among the first to show that mental disorders can be as burdensome as, or more burdensome than, some physical illnesses. Over that period, global anorexia and bulimia cases rose 71 per cent. As general background, eating disorders have long been seen as more common in wealthy Western countries, and Dr Santomauro noted that higher prevalence in high-income settings is usual.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **Researchers:** Dr Santomauro says Australia's lead may partly reflect different survey methods, but not entirely.
- **Clinicians:** Sarah Cox says the study confirms what families and health workers have reported for years, and Australia may simply detect the problem better.
- **Lived experience:** Jeanette Chan says eating disorders are often framed in Western terms, making it harder for migrants to recognise and seek help, and that investment hasn't been enough.
- **Limitations:** the study has gaps in bulimia mortality data and less information from low-income countries, and excludes binge eating disorder and other common conditions.

## What to Watch
- Whether governments boost funding for prevention and early treatment.
- The fast relative growth in East Asia, South Asia and South-East Asia.
- Research into social media's role and into eating disorders beyond anorexia and bulimia.

concepts.context: This new eating disorder data comes from it.

To capture people who might not have access to treatment

OCEANIA.background_beginner: Eating disorders are mental illnesses where someone develops an unhealthy relationship with food, eating or their body. The two best-known are anorexia (eating far too little) and bulimia (bingeing then trying to undo it). They mostly affect young people and females, and can be life-threatening. Researchers, doctors, support services like the Butterfly Foundation, and governments are the main players. The topic keeps coming up because cases have been rising for decades, possibly linked to body image pressures from social media, and because many people struggle to get affordable, timely care, especially outside big cities.
OCEANIA.description: A major global study published in JAMA Psychiatry found Australia has the highest rate of anorexia and bulimia in the world, while global cases have risen 71 per cent since 1990.

OCEANIA.title: ‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care laws
OCEANIA.simplified_title: Australia moves to ban AI chatbots that fake emotional closeness with kids
OCEANIA.quick_summary: Australia's digital duty of care bill, which would ban AI chatbots from fostering children's emotional dependence, has passed the lower house and now faces an uncertain Senate.
OCEANIA.simplified_body:
The federal government's digital duty of care bill passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday. It would place an overarching obligation on social media, games, apps and chatbots to provide a safe online environment. Labor accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney adding a ban on chatbot "material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy" and encourages a child's dependence on it instead of human relationships.

This affects big tech platforms and every Australian who uses them, especially kids. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said stories of people calling a chatbot their best friend should be a "wake up call". Platforms would also have to offer an easy, prominent "opt-out" from their algorithm and suggested content. Communications Minister Anika Wells says harmful content like material promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured.

The bill replaces a patchwork of existing online codes with one broad duty. The Coalition and One Nation voted against it, calling it "Orwellian" censorship, which Wells strongly denies. The Greens support it but want it tougher, including the right to sue platforms and bigger penalties.

The Senate will debate it in coming weeks, and a Greens inquiry reports back in late November. The government hopes to pass it by the end of 2026. A big sticking point is whether the telecommunications industry ombudsman should become a complaints watchdog for big tech. Labor rejected that idea in the lower house, but the Greens will push it in the Senate, and the ombudsman herself says her office is well placed to do it.
OCEANIA.why_it_matters: It could change how chatbots and social media are allowed to treat Australian kids, and may give everyday users somewhere to complain when platforms ignore them.
OCEANIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
As background, Australia has positioned itself as a world leader in online safety regulation, with an eSafety Commissioner and a social media minimum age for under-16s. This bill shifts from a list of specific codes to a broad "duty of care", a concept borrowed from negligence law, putting the onus on platforms to prevent harm.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **Labor** says platforms must take responsibility and remains open to Coalition amendments.
- **Coalition and One Nation** call it "Orwellian" censorship and voted against it.
- **Greens** back it but want private legal action, higher penalties and an external complaints body.
- **Independents** Kate Chaney won chatbot and opt-out amendments; Sophie Scamps's ombudsman amendment was rejected.
- **Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert** says without an external pathway, users risk being stuck with automated responses that "don't go anywhere".

## What to Watch
- The Greens' Senate inquiry report in late November.
- Whether the Coalition shifts or Labor relies on the Greens and crossbench.
- Whether an ombudsman role for big tech is added.
- How "simulates emotional intimacy" would be defined and enforced.

concepts.definition: A legal obligation requiring platforms to take reasonable steps to keep users safe, rather than just following a checklist of rules.
concepts.context: It's the core of the bill, replacing several existing online codes.

concepts.definition: An independent body that resolves complaints between consumers and phone or internet providers, funded by industry.
concepts.context: Some want its powers expanded to handle complaints against big tech.

concepts.context: The bill requires it to be easy to use and prominently available.

options: It has no algorithm opt-out
It only applies to games
Users have no external place to take unresolved complaints against platforms
It doesn't cover chatbots
quiz.explanation: Gebert praised the bill's onus on platforms but said people need somewhere to go when platforms don't resolve complaints.

OCEANIA.background_beginner: Governments worldwide are wrestling with how to make the internet safer, especially for kids. The main players are big tech companies like social media platforms and AI chatbot makers, governments writing new rules, and parents and advocates worried about harm. Australia has been especially active, creating online safety watchdogs and age rules. Recently AI chatbots that chat like a friend have raised new worries about children forming attachments to them. The debate keeps returning because it pits child safety against concerns about free speech and censorship, and technology keeps changing faster than laws can keep up.
OCEANIA.description: Australia's digital duty of care bill, which would ban AI chatbots from fostering children's emotional dependence, has passed the lower house and now faces an uncertain Senate.

OCEANIA.title: Actor's death may be first confirmed fatality linked to unapproved peptides
OCEANIA.simplified_title: Coroner links actor Richard Norton's death to unapproved peptide injections
OCEANIA.quick_summary: A Victorian coroner found Australian actor and martial artist Richard Norton's 2025 death was triggered by injecting unapproved peptides, and urged the medicines regulator to consider tougher rules.
OCEANIA.simplified_body:
A coroner has found that Australian actor, stuntman and martial artist Richard Norton, 75, died in March 2025 after a cardiac arrest triggered by injecting two unapproved peptides, CJC1295 and Ipamorelin. Coroner David Ryan found Norton had been taking more than his prescribed dose; he'd told a clinic nurse he was using double. Hours after that conversation he collapsed, and he died at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital on March 30, 2025. It's believed to be the first confirmed death in Australia from unapproved peptide use.

The peptides were prescribed by Dr Jerzy Muchnicki and made up by a licensed compounding pharmacy in Queensland. Norton signed a consent form and was told the treatment was experimental. The Medical Board of Australia (MBA) found Dr Muchnicki's clinical care met a reasonable standard but his notes were inadequate. He received a caution and conditions on his practice, and he apologised.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids, and some are marketed for things like muscle recovery and fatigue. Unapproved ones haven't been assessed by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), Australia's medicines regulator, for safety, quality or effectiveness. An expert who reviewed the case for the MBA said there's insufficient evidence CJC1295/Ipamorelin is safe or effective for humans. Even so, there are legal pathways that let doctors access them.

The coroner recommended the TGA review the benefits and risks of these peptides and consider further restrictions. The TGA says it keeps warning consumers and is considering whether more regulatory measures are needed.
OCEANIA.why_it_matters: Peptide therapy is popular in Australia's wellness and fitness scene, and this case shows doctors can legally prescribe products with no proven safety record, which could now prompt tighter national rules.
OCEANIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
As background, peptides have become a fixture in anti-ageing, bodybuilding and wellness circles, often promoted online. In Australia, the TGA approves medicines, but there are pathways that allow practitioners to access unapproved products, and compounding pharmacies can make up individual preparations. Norton's case is believed to be the first confirmed Australian death from unapproved peptide use.

## Multiple Perspectives
The coroner found the death was triggered by the peptides and that Norton exceeded his prescribed dose. The MBA's expert, Professor Alistair Vickery, said the clinical care was at a reasonably expected standard given the consent and Norton's prior peptide use, but the record keeping was below standard. Dr Muchnicki accepted accountability and apologised. The TGA says it has warned consumers and practitioners and is weighing further action. Some might argue adults should be free to try experimental treatments with informed consent; others will point to the lack of evidence on safety.

## What to Watch
Whether the TGA tightens access to peptides like CJC1295 and Ipamorelin, any changes to how compounding pharmacies supply them, and whether medical regulators issue new guidance to doctors offering peptide therapy.

concepts.context: Norton injected unapproved peptides for fatigue, recovery and muscle loss.

concepts.definition: A pharmacy that custom-makes medicines for an individual patient rather than supplying mass-produced products.
concepts.context: A Queensland compounding pharmacy made Norton's peptide injections.

concepts.definition: When the heart suddenly stops pumping blood effectively.
concepts.context: Norton suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting the peptides.

quiz.question: Why did the coroner recommend the TGA consider tougher restrictions?
options: Because the doctor failed to get any consent from Norton
Because the peptides were illegal imports bought online
Because the pharmacy was unlicensed
Because the peptides haven't been shown to be safe or effective, yet doctors can still access them
quiz.explanation: The peptides were legally prescribed and made by a licensed pharmacy with signed consent, but they're unapproved and lack evidence of safety, so the coroner asked the TGA to review them.

OCEANIA.background_beginner: Peptides are small protein-like molecules. Some are sold as treatments promising better recovery, more muscle or less tiredness, especially in gyms and wellness clinics. In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration decides which medicines are proven safe enough to approve, but doctors can still prescribe some unapproved products through special pathways. Richard Norton was a well-known Australian martial artist and screen stuntman who used these peptides. His death has become a test case, raising the question of whether popular but unproven treatments are too easy to get, and whether regulators need to step in more firmly.
OCEANIA.description: A Victorian coroner found Australian actor and martial artist Richard Norton's 2025 death was triggered by injecting unapproved peptides, and urged the medicines regulator to consider tougher rules.

OCEANIA.title: Menindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deaths
OCEANIA.simplified_title: Menindee Lakes hit five-year low, raising fears of summer fish kills
OCEANIA.quick_summary: Water at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales has dropped to its lowest level in five years, triggering irrigation restrictions as experts warn of mass fish deaths this summer.
OCEANIA.simplified_body:
Combined water storage at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales (NSW) fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the lowest since 2021. In the upper lakes, volumes dropped below 250GL, which automatically triggers temporary restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin.

Those restrictions limit how much some irrigators can take, so water is saved for critical human needs and the environment. The big worry is the fish. Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University says officials are predicting "with a level of certainty" that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer unless more water flows down the Darling-Baaka River.

Menindee has been here before: catastrophic fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023 left millions of dead fish along the river. After the 2023 state election, Premier Chris Minns promised an investigation. An expert panel under the northern basin connectivity program recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods to keep water flowing to Menindee. It delivered its final report two years ago, but the government hasn't implemented it yet.

What happens next depends largely on the weather. Local resident Graeme McCrabb says small inflows from recent Queensland rain offer some hope, but more is needed, and without it the risk would be "very high" in January or February. A milder summer would help. Comment has been sought from NSW water minister Rose Jackson.
OCEANIA.why_it_matters: The Darling-Baaka is a lifeline for outback NSW towns and ecosystems, and repeated fish kills have become a national symbol of how Australia shares scarce river water between farms, communities and nature.
OCEANIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
Menindee Lakes saw mass fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023, with millions of fish dying along the Darling-Baaka. As general background, these events are usually linked to low flows, heat and algal blooms that strip oxygen from the water. After the 2023 kills, the NSW government set up an expert panel under the northern basin connectivity program, which recommended curbing upstream overextraction during dry spells. Its final report came out two years ago but hasn't been implemented.

## Multiple Perspectives
Scientists like Prof Jamie Pittock want a major rainfall event plus state governments stopping irrigators pumping out the "first flush" of water. Local resident Graeme McCrabb says agencies have made "no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes" since the fish kills. The restrictions now in place do limit some irrigators, reflecting the competing needs of agriculture, towns and the environment. The NSW government's response hadn't been given at the time of reporting.

## What to Watch
- Whether Queensland inflows reach Menindee in meaningful amounts.
- Summer temperatures, especially in January and February.
- Signs of green algal blooms in the lakes.
- Whether the government acts on the connectivity panel's recommendations.

OCEANIA.background_beginner: Menindee Lakes are a group of lakes near the small town of Menindee in outback New South Wales, fed by the Darling River, also known by its Aboriginal name, the Baaka. The river is part of the huge Murray-Darling system that supplies water to farms, towns and wildlife across south-eastern Australia. Upstream, irrigators pump water for crops like cotton, while downstream communities and the environment depend on what's left. During droughts, the river can slow to a trickle, and in recent years low water and heat have caused enormous fish deaths. Locals, scientists and governments keep arguing over how to share the water fairly, so the issue returns every dry summer.
OCEANIA.description: Water at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales has dropped to its lowest level in five years, triggering irrigation restrictions as experts warn of mass fish deaths this summer.

ASIA.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
ASIA.simplified_title: China now supports more elderly people than children for the first time
ASIA.quick_summary: Official Chinese data show the share of dependent elderly people relative to working-age adults (23%) has overtaken the share for children (22%) for the first time.
ASIA.simplified_body:
China's National Bureau of Statistics has released data showing that, for the first time, the country's old-age dependency ratio (23%) is higher than its child dependency ratio (22%). In plain terms, working-age people are now supporting more elderly people than kids. More than 223 million people in China are aged 65 and over, nearly 16% of the population, compared with about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

This matters for families, who have fewer young people to look after ageing relatives, and for the government, which faces rising costs for pensions, healthcare and long-term care. Analysts say it could also slow growth in the world's second largest economy and reduce people's spending power. On the flip side, the state-controlled Global Times points to a growing 'silver economy' serving older consumers, many of whom are healthier and wealthier than earlier generations.

The shift comes from longer life expectancy, rapid urbanisation and the one-child policy, which ran from 1980 to the end of 2015. The government estimates it prevented about 400 million births, though that figure is contested. Even after the rules eased, birth rates have hit historic lows, with rising living costs, higher education levels and changing gender roles all playing a part.

Beijing has written more support for older people into its latest five-year economic blueprint, and more than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior allowances by the end of 2025. Expect more public spending to shift from schools towards pensions and healthcare. Some experts also question the dependency ratio itself, arguing it wrongly labels many capable older people as dependants.
ASIA.why_it_matters: China's shrinking workforce is closely watched because it could affect global growth, and China is Australia's biggest trading partner, so a slower Chinese economy can ripple through to Australian exports.
ASIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
The one-child policy (1980 to end of 2015) was introduced to slow rapid population growth. As general background, China later moved to allow two and then three children, but the article notes birth rates have still fallen to historic lows. Large past birth cohorts, especially people born from the 1950s to 1970s, are now reaching old age just as fewer young people follow them.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **Government/state media:** The Global Times frames it as entry into a 'moderately ageing society', a long-term historical trend that brings strain but also opportunity in the silver economy.
- **Economists/sociologists:** Mu Zheng (National University of Singapore) warns it may limit economic growth and spending power and challenge China's ambitions.
- **Critics of the measure:** Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) calls the milestone 'symbolic' and says the dependency ratio risks 'taking agency away' from older people and ignores healthcare improvements.
- The government's 400 million prevented-births estimate is contested.

## What to Watch
- How the five-year blueprint's aged-care measures are funded and rolled out.
- Whether birth rates respond to pro-marriage and pro-family campaigns.
- Shifts in public spending from education to pensions and healthcare.
- Growth of the silver economy and its effect on consumer demand.

concepts.definition: A measure comparing people usually not working (children or the elderly) with the working-age population.
concepts.context: China's old-age dependency ratio hit 23%, overtaking the child ratio of 22%.

concepts.definition: A Chinese rule from 1980 to the end of 2015 that limited most families to one child.
concepts.context: It is a major reason there are now fewer young people to support older relatives.

concepts.definition: Businesses and services aimed at older consumers.
concepts.context: State media say ageing creates opportunities here as well as costs.

quiz.question: Why does the new data suggest more Chinese public spending may shift towards pensions and healthcare?
options: Because China's total population suddenly grew
Because the one-child policy was reintroduced in 2025
Because the share of dependent elderly people now exceeds that of dependent children
Because children now make up 16% of the population
quiz.explanation: With elderly dependants (23%) now outnumbering child dependants (22%) relative to workers, spending needs move from schools to aged care, pensions and health.

ASIA.background_beginner: China has the world's second largest economy and one of its largest populations. In 1980 the government brought in the one-child policy to slow fast population growth, and it lasted until the end of 2015. Combined with people living longer and moving to cities, this means China now has lots of older people and relatively few young ones. Even after relaxing the rules, the government has struggled to get couples to have more babies because of costs and changing lifestyles. The topic keeps coming up because fewer workers supporting more retirees affects pensions, healthcare, family life and economic growth, both in China and around the world.
ASIA.description: Official Chinese data show the share of dependent elderly people relative to working-age adults (23%) has overtaken the share for children (22%) for the first time.

ASIA.title: North Korea fires several missiles amid growing tensions with South Korea
ASIA.simplified_title: North Korea fires about 10 missiles as border tensions with South rise
ASIA.quick_summary: North Korea launched around 10 short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its east coast on Thursday, adding to a tense stand-off with South Korea over landmines and the border.
ASIA.simplified_body:
North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said. They were launched at about 12:30 pm local time from near Wonsan. Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles landed outside Japan's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), the stretch of sea where a country controls fishing and resources.

The launch comes as relations between the two Koreas sour. On September 21, three South Korean soldiers were hurt by landmines in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the buffer strip dividing the countries. A joint South Korea–United Nations investigation found North Korea planted the mines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago. Pyongyang (North Korea's government) denies it and has warned of retaliation. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called Seoul's demand for an apology "despicable" and rejected its offer of medical equipment.

North Korea has tested missiles on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently on October 12, the day after United States (US) President Donald Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un. Trump's outreach has raised worries that South Korea, a key US ally, could be sidelined in any nuclear talks.

South Korea says it's boosting surveillance and sharing information with the US and Japan. North Korea has announced plans to restart propaganda broadcasts and deploy new weapons near the border, while Seoul has proposed talks to clarify the border and avoid accidental clashes. Pyongyang hasn't responded yet.
ASIA.why_it_matters: Every launch and border scare raises the risk of a miscalculation in a region that's vital to global trade, including for Australia, whose major trading partners Japan and South Korea sit right next door.
ASIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
As background: the Korean War (1950–53) ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the peninsula split along the DMZ. North Korea has built up nuclear and missile programs over decades, and Trump met Kim Jong Un in his first term without reaching a lasting deal. This article reports more than 10 rounds of tests this year.

## Multiple Perspectives
South Korea and the UN say North Korea planted the landmines that wounded three soldiers; Pyongyang denies it and threatens retaliation. Seoul wants an apology and border talks, while Kim Yo Jong has dismissed its demands. Meanwhile, Trump's overtures to Kim are seen by some as a chance for diplomacy, but they've also raised concerns that Seoul could be left out of any negotiations.

## What to Watch
- Whether North Korea answers Seoul's offer of border talks.
- The resumption of propaganda broadcasts and new weapons deployments near the border.
- Any concrete moves towards a Trump–Kim meeting, and whether South Korea gets a seat at the table.
- Further missile launches timed around diplomatic signals.

ASIA.background_beginner: Korea was split into North and South after World War II, and the two sides fought a war in the 1950s that ended in a ceasefire, not a peace deal. They've been technically at war ever since. North Korea is a secretive state led by Kim Jong Un, and it keeps testing missiles to show off its military strength and pressure its neighbours and the United States. South Korea is a close US ally, with Japan nearby also on alert. Tests, border incidents and on-off talks with US leaders like Donald Trump keep this rivalry in the news.
ASIA.description: North Korea launched around 10 short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its east coast on Thursday, adding to a tense stand-off with South Korea over landmines and the border.

ASIA.title: Indonesian students protest rising prices, government’s handling of forest fires
ASIA.simplified_title: Indonesian students protest prices, subsidy cuts and forest fire response
ASIA.quick_summary: Hundreds of Indonesian students marched in Jakarta on Wednesday (Oct 28) against rising prices, shrinking subsidies and the government's handling of wildfires, but were blocked by a heavy security presence.
ASIA.simplified_body:
Hundreds of students from universities and not-for-profit groups took to the streets of Jakarta, Indonesia's capital, on Wednesday (Oct 28). They carried banners criticising President Prabowo Subianto's policies and used the hashtag #IndonesiaAware. Police and military, backed by armoured vehicles, blocked them from gathering at the Hotel Indonesia roundabout and marching about 3km to the Presidential Palace. There were a few minor scuffles.

The students want wildfires in Sumatra and Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo) declared a national disaster. They also want the government to stop spending on populist programmes like Prabowo's free meals scheme, which they say drains money from disaster mitigation and infrastructure. They're angry about energy subsidies being cut from 376.8 trillion rupiah this year to 261 trillion rupiah next year, while petrol prices climb and subsidised fuel is scarce because of tensions in the Middle East.

Some background: the free school meals budget this year is 229 trillion rupiah (US$12.6 billion), down from 268 trillion. Meanwhile the National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) was told in February it would get only 491 billion rupiah for 2026, a nearly 75 per cent drop. After several disasters, its regular funding this year was raised to 1.08 trillion rupiah, plus 4.62 trillion in emergency funds. The protest fell on Youth Pledge Day, which marks a 1928 declaration of unity by young Indonesians.

Prabowo's approval ratings have fallen steadily since late last year, according to SMRC surveys. Protests have also happened in haze-hit areas of Borneo and Sumatra, and there was a major protest in August in which hundreds were detained. More demonstrations seem likely if prices keep rising and the fires continue.
ASIA.why_it_matters: Indonesia is Australia's huge next-door neighbour, so its political stability matters to the region, and smoke from its forest fires has a history of drifting across borders.
ASIA.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
Student movements have long shaped Indonesian politics. As general background, student-led protests helped bring down Suharto in 1998. The timing on Youth Pledge Day, which commemorates a 1928 unity declaration by young Indonesians, gives this protest symbolic weight. More recently, weeks-long nationwide protests in 2025 followed the police killing of a motorcycle taxi driver, and several more people died during that unrest. Another major protest in August saw hundreds detained.

## Multiple Perspectives
Students argue that flagship programmes like free school meals and village cooperatives are wasteful and crowd out disaster mitigation, while energy subsidy cuts hit people already facing high petrol prices. As one student put it, the subsidy cut came while the government earmarked more money for such programmes. The government has trimmed the free meals budget from 268 trillion to 229 trillion rupiah, with officials saying more cuts were possible, and lifted BNPB's funding after several disasters, though it remains far below the meals budget. Authorities chose to block the march; protesters say this breached their freedom of expression.

## What to Watch
- Whether the government declares the Sumatra and Kalimantan fires a national disaster.
- Further cuts to the free meals budget or changes to energy subsidies.
- Prabowo's approval ratings in future SMRC surveys.
- Whether protests spread or turn violent, as in 2025.

concepts.definition: Government money that keeps fuel and power prices lower for consumers.
concepts.context: Indonesia plans to cut them from 376.8 trillion to 261 trillion rupiah, which could push up costs.

concepts.context: Students want the wildfires in Sumatra and Kalimantan declared one.

concepts.context: Protesters single out Prabowo's free meals scheme as an example.
